# Selling motion films to businesses

Research snapshot: September 2026, US market. Prices are public listings and case studies. They show that buying categories exist, not that any buyer will purchase *your* offer. Re-verify before quoting.

## Positioning

- Sell the **business job a video does**: explain the service, earn quote requests, follow up on quotes, refresh ads monthly. Don't sell "AI video".
- Target buyers who **already spend on marketing and already have footage**: established contractors, multi-property operators, and the agencies serving them.
- The client's real footage is the proof. AI-generated imagery is for concepts, supporting shots and pitches, always labelled.
- The commodity tier is crowded ($30 AI tools, $150 reels). Differentiate on judgment, accuracy to the client's real business, quality control, and fast variants.

## Verticals

| Vertical | What to sell | Buying evidence | Caveats |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Roofing / home services** | Project stories, process explainers, objection handling, quote follow-up, monthly ad variants | Roof Lens: 10 short videos for $1,500/month from client footage, incl. publishing, quarterly commitment (rooflens.com/pricing). Tasca Studios: $7,500 roofing project incl. filming, drone and graphics (tascastudios.com/video-case-studies/neumann-roofing) | The package price isn't transaction volume; the $7.5k project includes filming |
| **Apartment operators / property agencies** | Floor-plan explainers, leasing ads, amenity videos, availability/offer variants | Legend Management commissioned 285 unit tour videos (Grace Hill/Realync case). Conversion Logix lease-up campaign used YouTube + social video (48 leases, multi-channel). Focus Media lists a +$150 property-reel add-on | Tours were filmed; the lease result isn't video-only. Sell to multi-property operators or agencies, not single agents |
| **Ecommerce** | Product demos, feature animations, product-page clips, ad-hook variants | Soona: 15–30s product highlight video $455/SKU + studio fee. Creatify/Vitals: $30 AI add-on, 1,000+ creatives/month (vendor-reported) | Cheap AI substitutes exist; generic image animation won't stand out |
| **B2B software** | Sales explainers, onboarding, feature updates, customer education | Vidico/Brightflow (explainer + onboarding + brand). HoneyBook reported +9% waitlist signups in an A/B test (vendor-hosted) | Needs real product access; best fit for fully code-built motion |
| **Solar** (later) | Installation-process or FAQ explainer | Boston Solar/Energy Circle: one 90s film cut into three short ads (2019–20) | Historical; savings claims need current, local, approved numbers |

A good first test is roofing/home services: a close competitor offer exists to price against, the buyer is clear, the sales use is concrete (help a homeowner understand the job before a quote), and there are no financial claims. For a showcase built entirely in code, a B2B software workflow explainer is the easiest fit.

## Pilot offer template

- One core 20–30s film + two opening hooks + two aspect ratios (16:9, 9:16) = four exports.
- One consolidated revision round.
- The client supplies approved footage, service area, process facts and CTA. Filming, ad spend, publishing and campaign management are separate line items.
- Time your real production and revisions before setting a price.
- First success test: does the buyer pay and use it? Lead quality and booked jobs need their campaign/CRM data later.

## Price anchors (Sept 2026)

$30 AI add-on · $150 property reel · $455 product clip · $1,500/month for 10-video retainer · $7,500 custom project with filming. The defensible middle is probably recurring, business-specific creative, not one-off generic clips (a hypothesis to test).

## Honesty rules for sales material

- Never present AI imagery as a real completed job, customer or result.
- No invented testimonials, ratings, savings, warranties or performance lifts.
- Vendor case-study numbers are vendor claims; say so if you cite them.
- Label concept films as concept films.

## Unknowns to validate with real buyers

Customer acquisition cost, close rate, production margin with client footage, whether a remote motion offer beats local videographers or in-house phone footage, and which vertical converts best.
